title: Find Longest Awesome Substring
statement:
The string `s` is made of decimal digits. Call a non-empty contiguous piece of `s` **awesome** if its characters can be reordered, using as many swaps as you like, into a palindrome.

Return the length of the longest awesome substring of `s`.
notes:
## Intuition

A multiset of characters can be arranged into a palindrome exactly when at most one character occurs an odd number of times. Testing every substring with its own counts is O(n²) or worse. Only the parity of each digit's count matters, and ten parities fit in a 10-bit `mask`. Keep the mask of every prefix: the substring between two prefixes has the XOR of their masks as its parity pattern. So a substring ending at `i` is awesome when the earlier prefix's mask equals the current one, or differs from it in exactly one bit. To make it as long as possible, remember the **first** index where each mask appeared.

## Approach

1. Create `firstIndex` with 1024 slots, all `Infinity` (never seen), and set `firstIndex[0] = -1` for the empty prefix.
2. For each index `i`, flip the bit of digit `s[i]` in `mask`.
3. If the same mask appeared before, the substring after it has all even counts: try `i - firstIndex[mask]`.
4. For each `digit`, an earlier mask differing only in that bit gives one odd count: try `i - firstIndex[mask ^ (1 << digit)]`.
5. Record `i` as the first index of `mask` if it is new, and return `best` at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "3242415"`. After `'3'` the mask is `{3}` (first seen at 0); after `'2'` it is `{2,3}`; after `'4'` it is `{2,3,4}`.

- `i = 3` (`'2'`): mask `{3,4}`; flipping digit 4 gives `{3}`, first seen at 0, so `"242"` has length `3`.
- `i = 4` (`'4'`): mask `{3}` again; flipping digit 3 gives the empty mask at `-1`, so `"32424"` has length `5`.
- `i = 5` (`'1'`): mask `{1,3}`; flipping digit 1 gives `{3}` at 0, so `"24241"` also has length `5`.
- `i = 6` (`'5'`): nothing longer appears.

The answer is `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(10 · n): each character checks the current mask and its ten neighbours.
- Space: O(2^10) for `firstIndex`, independent of `n`.

## Pitfalls

- Seed the empty prefix (`firstIndex[0] = -1`), or substrings starting at index 0 are missed.
- Store only the first index of a mask; overwriting it with later indices shortens the answers.
- Check both the equal mask (all counts even) and the ten one-bit neighbours (one odd count).
- Never-seen masks must not produce a length; `Infinity` makes `i - Infinity` negative so `Math.max` ignores it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `firstIndex` | for each parity mask, the earliest prefix end where it occurred |
| `mask` | parity of every digit's count in `s[0..i]` |
| `best` | longest awesome substring found so far |
| `i` | index of the current character, the right end of the substring |
| `digit` | the digit allowed to have an odd count |

narration.2: One slot per possible parity mask of the ten digits; Infinity means not seen yet.
narration.3: The empty prefix, ending before index 0, has every count even.
narration.4: mask holds the parity of each digit's count in the prefix read so far.
narration.7: Extend the prefix one character at a time.
narration.8: Flip the parity bit of this digit.
narration.9: An earlier prefix with the same mask leaves a substring whose counts are all even.
narration.10: Try letting each digit be the one with an odd count.
narration.11: An earlier mask differing only in that digit's bit leaves exactly one odd count.
narration.13: Keep only the earliest index for this mask so later substrings are as long as possible.
narration.15: Return the longest awesome length found.
